result:
The final pick scores **66.6× on the search split** (median of three scorer runs: 67.7, 66.4 and 66.6), against about 1.0 for the baseline. It used **13 of the 24 scorer calls**. On my own held-out seeds it ran 64.7× faster, close to its search-split result. It is saved as `final.py`.

| | Local harness, search seeds | Scorer (search split) | Local held-out seeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 1.0 | 0.997 | 1.0 |
| First answer (`c1_prefix.py`) | 39.4 | 31.7 | – |
| Search A's pick (`a/pick.py`) | 54.8 | 48.1 / 47.7 / 47.5 → 47.7 | 47.4 |
| **Search B's pick → `final.py`** | 68.5 | 67.7 / 66.4 / 66.6 → **66.6** | **64.7** |

**Why it's faster.** The baseline checks every session against every window. The first answer and search A's pick both sort all session starts and ends and then do 4 binary searches per window. The final pick does less work:
- It sorts only the window edges, at most about 2 × 500 values, so the thousands of sessions are never sorted.
- Each session is placed between two window edges with one binary search, and adds its rate and an offset at the points where it starts and stops counting. A session that ends before the next window edge adds a single total, and sessions with a rate of 0 add only to the counts.
- Running totals then give the usage up to each window edge as a simple formula. A window's usage is the value at its end minus the value at its start. Its count is the sessions that start before the window ends, minus those that end at or before it begins.

**Correctness.** It matches the reference on the harness's 400+ small edge cases and on the large inputs. It also matched on a separate 3,000-case random test (`fuzz.py`) covering very large rates, negative rates, heavily repeated coordinates and more windows than sessions, and it always returns plain integers.

**Approaches tried in the two independent searches** (each search's full log is in `a/notes.md` and `b/notes.md`):
- **Search A** stayed with sorting starts and ends plus running totals, and mostly varied how the sort is done. Other ideas were slower than its best of 54.8:
  - one combined sort of all start and end points: 46.9
  - packing several values into single integers: 31–40
  - summing rates per point in dictionaries: 33.6
  - merging two separately sorted lists: 40.2
- **Search B** moved to the window-edge buckets, which reached 60.9 on the first try, then added the two shortcuts for short and zero-rate sessions. Other ideas were also slower:
  - one sort of all start and end events: 36.8
  - packing values into big integers: 34–52
  - a lookup grid instead of binary search: 60.0
  - doing the per-session work through built-in map calls: 49.7–58.6
- **Pattern in both searches:** any trick that made integers much larger slowed things down.

Two departures from the method:
- **Search A stopped early.** It quit after one round without improvement instead of two, leaving 7 of its 10 calls unused. Search B followed the stopping rule.
- **Search A tuned on extra inputs I can't check.** To time larger coordinate ranges it wrote its own script in `/tmp` using seeds 11–16, and I never saw those inputs. Neither search used the held-out seeds 101–104.

The candidate log is in `log.md`. My harness is `harness.py` (run `python3 harness.py <file> heldout` for the held-out seeds) and the random test is `fuzz.py`.

Separately, two connected services (claude.ai Atlassian Rovo and HyperFrames by HeyGen) need sign-in through claude.ai's connector settings before they can be used. This task didn't need either.
